name: Pinguecula / pterygium removal

card.summary: Surgery to remove the yellowish or pinkish conjunctival growths of pinguecula and pterygium, done mainly for medical reasons and sometimes for looks.
card.aka: Pterygium excision, pterygium surgery, surfer's eye surgery
card.note: Pterygium can recur after surgery, so technique and follow-up matter in the published studies.

quick.overview:
A pinguecula is a yellowish bump on the white of the eye, and a pterygium is a related fleshy, often pink growth that extends onto the cornea. Both are linked to long-term sun and dust exposure. Removal is a recognised eye operation, mostly for vision, irritation or contact lens problems, and some people seek it for cosmetic reasons.

The surgical literature is large for pterygium and focuses on recurrence rates, techniques and effects on corneal shape. Pinguecula removal has far less published research.
quick.mechanism: The growth is surgically excised. Modern techniques usually cover the bare area with tissue, most often a conjunctival autograft from the same eye, held with sutures or tissue glue, to reduce regrowth. Other approaches in the literature include amniotic membrane, mitomycin C and, historically, beta irradiation.
quick.risks: Recurrence is the main reported problem, with rates varying widely by technique and population; an encyclopedic summary says about half of cases recur, while grafting studies report lower figures. Other documented issues include corneal astigmatism changes and complications of adjunct treatments such as radiation.

lead: Pinguecula and pterygium removal is eye surgery that takes away raised growths on the white of the eye. A pinguecula is a yellowish bump on the conjunctiva, and a pterygium is a related pink, fleshy, roughly triangular growth that extends onto the cornea; the latter is sometimes called surfer's eye.[1][2] Both are associated with ultraviolet light, wind and dust exposure.[1][19]

For appearance, the point is a clearer, whiter-looking eye. Persistent redness and a visible wedge of tissue are among the features that bother people about these growths, and Wikipedia lists cosmetic appearance as a common concern alongside irritation and contact lens discomfort.[1] Some studies of extended removal with extended conjunctival transplantation report cosmesis alongside recurrence.[7][8]

Many growths need no surgery, and artificial tears are commonly used for irritation.[1][3] When removal is performed, the research literature compares techniques such as bare sclera excision, conjunctival autografting, amniotic membrane transplantation, mitomycin C and radiation, with recurrence as the central outcome.[3][4][6] Pterygium surgery has a large literature; pinguecula removal has far less.

paras: A pterygium is a benign growth of conjunctiva onto the cornea, often starting on the nasal side. Its exact cause is unknown, but UV exposure, dust and genetic factors are implicated, and prevalence varies from about 1% to 33% depending on region [1].
A pinguecula has similar histology but stays on the conjunctiva and does not extend onto the cornea [1].

Pterygium usually starts on the side of the eye nearest the nose, often affects both eyes and grows slowly; it rarely grows large enough to cover the pupil. Reported symptoms include persistent redness, a foreign-body sensation, tearing, dryness and itching, and advanced cases can cause astigmatism and corneal scarring.[1] The tissue contains sun-damaged (elastotic) collagen and fibrovascular growth, and a line of iron deposits called Stocker's line can appear near its head.[1] Wikipedia notes the condition has been described since at least 1000 BC.[1]

A 2014 review found strong evidence linking UV exposure to pterygium, while evidence linking UV to pinguecula was described as more limited.[19] A study of 57 people with pinguecula measured tear flow, film stability and mucus against age-matched controls to examine how a pinguecula relates to the tear film.[20]

Surgeons list several reasons to remove a pterygium: vision affected by induced astigmatism or scarring, persistent irritation, contact lens intolerance, and appearance.[1][3] Because a pterygium is vascular tissue, it can look like a patch of persistent redness, and the cosmetic aim of surgery is an even, white-looking sclera.

The literature on extended removal followed by extended conjunctival transplantation explicitly reports cosmesis as an outcome in primary and recurrent cases.[7][8] Cosmetic-only removal of a pinguecula is rarely studied.

Bare sclera excision leaves the exposed area uncovered. Conjunctival autografting covers it with tissue from the same eye, and amniotic membrane transplantation is an alternative in extensive cases [1][6]. Extended removal followed by extended conjunctival transplantation has been studied for both primary and recurrent pterygium, including its cosmetic result [7][8]. Sliding conjunctival flaps have also been described [9]. Fixation with sutures or fibrin glue and the adjunct mitomycin C are subjects of comparison trials [10][11].

Bare sclera excision was historically common but had higher recurrence in early trials, which is one reason grafting became the dominant method.[6] Mitomycin C, applied to reduce regrowth, has been studied with tarsorrhaphy and with amniotic membrane and autograft in registered trials.[11][22] Beta irradiation after removal was used in the past, and a long-term series reported recurrence and complications over more than a decade.[4][13]

In an early randomised trial in the Caribbean, recurrence was 21% in 19 grafted cases versus 37% in 16 bare sclera cases, a difference that was not statistically significant, and younger age was strongly associated with recurrence [6]. A review of 161 recurrences examined how long patients must be followed to capture recurrence [12]. A long-term series of beta irradiation after removal reported recurrence and complications over more than a decade of follow-up [13].

A Cochrane review summarised in an encyclopedic source found autograft less likely to recur at six months than amniotic membrane transplant, while the effect of adding mitomycin C was unclear [1]. A 2021 review notes that pterygium can induce corneal irregularity and astigmatism and that removal can change refractive properties [3].

Clinical research is substantial for pterygium surgery, including randomised and prospective studies of recurrence [6][7][8] and registered trials comparing mini-SLET with limbal-conjunctival autograft [14], sutured versus sutureless autograft [15], glue versus sutures [10], and mitomycin C with amniotic membrane [11]. Studies of corneal effects include analyses of astigmatism induced by pterygium [16][17] and a registered trial of topographic changes after surgery [18]. No studies found specifically addressed cosmetic-only removal of a pinguecula.

The 1989 Caribbean randomised trial compared 19 grafted with 16 bare-sclera eyes and reported 21% versus 37% recurrence, a difference that was not statistically significant.[6] A recurrence-time analysis of 161 cases examined how long follow-up must continue to capture recurrence.[12] Registered trials compare mini-SLET with limbal-conjunctival autograft (n=57), sutured with sutureless grafts (n=70), glue with sutures (n=40) and mitomycin C, amniotic membrane and autograft (n=750).[14][15][10][11]

Wikipedia reports that artificial tears relieve irritation, and that sunglasses with side shields, wide-brimmed hats and UV-blocking eye protection for water sports are suggested to help prevent formation or slow growth.[1] Topical indomethacin 0.1% solution was compared with dexamethasone in randomised studies of inflamed pterygium and pinguecula, which addressed redness and inflammation rather than removing the growth.[21]

Eye whiteness is part of how people discuss eye-area aesthetics, and a pinguecula or pterygium is among the structural causes of a discoloured or red-looking sclera. Surgery is discussed as an ophthalmic procedure carried out by eye surgeons, with recurrence and the look of the healing eye as the main appearance questions.

timeline.event: Pterygium described in early medical writing, according to Wikipedia.[1]
First reported randomised trial of conjunctival autografting for pterygium [6].
Long-term results of beta irradiation after pterygium removal published [13].
Prospective study of extended removal with extended conjunctival transplantation [8].
Review update on pathophysiology, clinical features and management published.[2]
